Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the principles of lower extremity limb deformity analysis.
Describe the proper techniques for using lower extremity radiographs in limb deformity
analysis.
Review the natural history of lower extremity alignment in the pediatric population and the
consequences of malalignment.
Introduction
The analysis of lower extremity alignment and deformity is an important component of the
orthopaedic care of children and adults.
Alignment is assessed in the coronal and sagittal planes and the rotational plane.

Lower extremity alignment determines the passage of the mechanical forces through the
lower extremities.
Malalignment of the lower extremities may cause difficulty in function, discomfort, and
degenerative changes.
Clinical Evaluation
The importance of a thorough patient history and physical examination cannot be
overemphasized. Surgeons must determine the etiology of the limb deformity. Common
etiologies include congenital limb deficiencies, congenital birth differences, postinfectious
deformities, posttraumatic deformities, and idiopathic deformities. The birth history may aid in
detecting potential underlying neurologic diagnoses, such as cerebral palsy. The medical and
surgical histories may help define the factors contributing to a limb deformity, such as prior
infections, trauma, or nutritional issues.
The family history is important and may identify underlying skeletal dysplasia; bone disease; or
hereditary neurologic issues, such as peripheral neuropathy. The physical examination
includes an assessment of the patient’s height and weight and evaluation of growth over time.
The upper extremities and the spine must be examined. Evaluation of the lower extremities
includes an assessment of joint range of motion and stability, assessment of the length of the
femoral and tibial segments, and a visual assessment of lower extremity alignment in the
coronal and sagittal planes.
The Galeazzi examination is used to measure femoral segment lengths, and a prone knee
flexed examination is used to measure tibial and foot segment lengths (Figure 1). Joint
contractures may masquerade as limb-length differences. A knee flexion contracture may
make a limb appear shorter when, in fact, the femoral and tibial segments are symmetric
lengths.
An equinus contracture may make the affected lower extremity appear longer if the patient is
standing because the foot is unable to achieve a plantigrade position. Gait may be observed
during an observational gait analysis conducted in a hallway or an open space or via a
quantitative gait laboratory analysis, if such a resource is available. Neurologic, vascular, and
skin status also must be examined.

Figure 1 Clinical photographs of two separate patients demonstrate the Galeazzi examination,
which is used to measure femoral segment lengths. A, The Galeazzi examination shows the left

Radiographic Evaluation
Well-positioned and executed radiographs are essential for accurate limb deformity analysis.
Orthogonal views of the lower extremities are used for the analysis of coronal and sagittal
plane limb alignment and surgical planning.
A full-length standing AP radiograph includes both lower extremities from the proximal aspect
of the iliac crest to the ankle.1 The patellae should point directly forward. The feet may not
point directly forward if internal or external tibial torsion is present. Blocks with increments of
0.5 cm may be placed under the foot of the shorter lower extremity to level the pelvis. The
height of the blocks must be noted on the radiograph (Figure 2).
A full-length standing lateral radiograph includes one lower extremity from the hip joint to the
ankle joint. The radiograph is obtained with the knee in maximum extension. The foot is
placed flat on the ground parallel to the cassette, and the heel is externally rotated 10° to

the leg of interest.1

with a lower extremity deformity with a block placed under the foot of the shorter extremity. A,
AP standing radiograph of bilateral lower extremities with the patellae directly forward, knees
fully extended, and a 9-cm block under the right foot to level the pelvis. B, Lateral long-leg
radiograph of the right lower extremity with the knee fully extended. (Courtesy of Jeanne M.
Franzone, MD, Wilmington, DE.)

The alignment of the lower extremity in the coronal plane is analyzed on a full-length standing
radiograph with the knee fully extended and the patella pointing directly forward and is
defined by the mechanical axis, which is a straight line connecting the center of the femoral
head to the center of the ankle.1,2 Mechanical axis deviation occurs if the mechanical axis does
not pass through the center of the knee.
The magnitude of mechanical axis deviation can be measured on a calibrated radiograph as
the number of millimeters from the center of the knee to the mechanical axis along a line
perpendicular to the mechanical axis. If the mechanical axis passes medial to the center of the
knee, the lower extremity is in varus; if the mechanical axis passes lateral to the center of the
knee, the lower extremity is in valgus (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Standing AP lower extremity radiographs demonstrate determination of mechanical
axis deviation. A, Radiograph of bilateral lower extremities of a 13-year-old girl with bilateral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:35 PM
AAOS | Lower Extremity Deformity Analysis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000597
5/21

genu valgus. The mechanical axis of the lower extremity is indicated by the red line from the
center of the femoral head to the center of the ankle and falls lateral to the center of the knee.
B, Radiograph of the bilateral lower extremities of a 20-year-old woman with severe bilateral
genu varum. The mechanical axis of the lower extremity (red line) falls medial to the center of
the knee. (Courtesy of Jeanne M. Franzone, MD, Wilmington, DE.)
The goal is for the mechanical axis to pass directly through the center of the knee to evenly
distribute the weight-bearing forces; however, the mechanical axis is considered normal if it is
within 3 mm of the center of the knee.1 Data available on this topic are varied. In a
retrospective study of 25 knees in adult patients of different ages, Paley et al3 found the
normal mechanical axis deviation to be 9.7 mm medial (± 6.8 mm). In another study of normal
lower limbs in individuals older than 60 years without any evidence of pathologic abnormality
of the knee, the mechanical axis deviation was 4.1 mm (± 4 mm).2
To determine the factors contributing to overall varus or valgus alignment of the lower
extremity, each of the bone segments (femur and tibia) must be analyzed separately. The
femur and the tibia each have a mechanical axis and an anatomic axis. The hip, knee, and
ankle each have a joint line that represents the plane of that joint in space. The intersection of
the joint line and the mechanical or anatomic femoral or tibial axis forms a joint angle. These
joint angles are the major factors that determine the overall alignment of the lower limb.1
The mechanical axis of a bone segment is as follows (Figure 4, A):
A line from the center of the proximal joint to the center of the distal joint
Always a straight line
Can be outside the bone
Conversely, the anatomic axis of a bone segment is as follows (Figure 4, B):
Mid-diaphyseal line of a bone
Can be curved or straight
Always is inside the bone1
For the femur, the distinction between the mechanical axis and the anatomic axis is
important because a difference of approximately 5° to 9° exists between the two axes in
normal femurs. Females and individuals with a short stature tend to have a difference
between the two axes on the higher end of the range. In addition, the femoral anatomic axis
exits medial to the exit point of the mechanical axis in the distal femur. Conversely, the
mechanical and anatomic axes of the tibia are parallel and close enough to colinear that, for

Figure 4 AP radiographs of a right femur demonstrate determination of the mechanical axis
(red line; A) and the anatomic axis (red line; B) of the femur. The red line connecting the
midpoint of the purple lines indicates the mid-diaphyseal line, or the anatomic axis, of the
femur. (Courtesy of Jeanne M. Franzone, MD, Wilmington, DE.)
To measure the joint angles, in addition to defining the mechanical and anatomic axes, the
joint line must be defined. The joint lines represent the position of a joint in space (Figure 5).
For the proximal femur, the joint line is defined as a line drawn from the center of the
femoral head to the proximal tip of the greater trochanter (Figure 5, A). In children with
unossified greater trochanters, this line is more difficult to draw precisely and may be
estimated.
For the distal femur, the joint line is defined as a line connecting the two distal most points of
the distal femoral condyles (Figure 5, B).

For the proximal tibia, the joint line is defined as a line connecting points on the mid-portion
of the medial and lateral tibial plateaus (Figure 5, C).
For the distal tibia, the joint line is defined as a line drawn across the distal tibial plafond1,2
(Figure 5, D).
Figure 5 AP radiographs demonstrate determination of the joint line. A, Radiograph of a hip
demonstrates the proximal femur joint line (red line). B, Radiograph of a knee demonstrates
the distal femur joint line (red line). C, Radiograph of a knee demonstrates the proximal tibia
joint line (red line). D, Radiograph of an ankle demonstrates the distal tibia joint line (red
line). (Courtesy of Jeanne M. Franzone, MD, Wilmington, DE.)
The joint angles represent the intersection of the mechanical or anatomic axes with the joint
lines (Figure 6).
“a” or “m” indicates anatomic or mechanical.
“M” or “L” indicates whether the angle is medial or lateral to the axis of the bone.

An abnormal joint angle indicates the bone or bones of interest in deformity.
Three additional frontal plane angles of interest exist1 (Figure 7).
Joint line convergence angle—The angle between the distal femur and proximal tibia joint
lines should fall within 0° to 2° unless a medial or lateral joint opening is present to elevate
the joint line convergence angle.
Neck-shaft angle—The axis of the femoral neck is created by connecting the center of the
femoral head to the center of the femoral neck. The angle between the axis of the femoral
neck and the anatomic axis of the femur is the neck-shaft angle, with a normal range of
124° to 136°. High values indicate coxa valga, and low values indicate coxa vara.
Femoral anatomic-mechanical angle—The femoral anatomic-mechanical angle is the angle
between the anatomic and mechanical axes of the femur. The normal range is 5° to 9°.
Figure 7 AP radiographs demonstrate frontal plane angles of interest (arrows). A,
Radiograph of a knee demonstrates the joint line convergence angle (JLCA). B, Radiograph
of a hip demonstrates the neck-shaft angle (NSA). C, Radiograph of a femur demonstrates
the femoral anatomic-mechanical angle (AMA). The normal value and the normal range are
included for each angle. (Courtesy of Jeanne M. Franzone, MD, Wilmington, DE.)

Deformity Analysis
Thus far, the analysis has identified the bone segment or segments that are contributing to the
malalignment of the lower extremity. The abnormal joint angle or joint angles indicate whether
the culprit is the femur, the tibia, or both bones. The next step in the analysis is to focus on
each of those segments to identify the apex or apices of the deformity.
To locate the apex of the deformity, surgeons must determine the axis for each bone segment.
The apex is the intersection of the axis of each segment. Each apex has a magnitude in
degrees.1
The axis of a segment can be determined via three methods1 (Figure 8 ).
Mid-diaphyseal line—To ensure that a hidden deformity is not present closer to the joint, the
joint lines and angles should be drawn and measured. This method may be used only if the
segment includes a sufficient length of diaphyseal bone to draw an axis.
Normal joint angle or the contralateral joint angle if the contralateral side is unaffected—This
method is helpful if the deformity is close to a joint and the mid-diaphyseal technique is not
feasible.
Extended axis from the adjacent segment—This technique may be used only if the adjacent
bone segment is without substantial deformity. The technique also is helpful in patients with
a deformity close to a joint and may aid in matching the bone undergoing correction to the
other segment so that the postcorrection mechanical axis passes through the center of the
knee (or the desired point, such as the Fujisawa point).4

Figure 8 AP radiographs of a right lower extremity demonstrate the three methods used to
determine the axis of a segment. A, Mid-diaphyseal line. B, Normal joint angle. C, The
extended axis from the adjacent segment of that bone, which is without substantial
deformity. (Courtesy of Jeanne M. Franzone, MD, Wilmington, DE.)
The osteotomy is planned as close as possible to the apex of the deformity, with
considerations for the anatomy and biology of the area. For example, proximal tibia
osteotomies are performed distal to the tubercle; however, the apex often is much closer to
the proximal tibia joint surface in patients with Blount disease. In another example, distal
femur osteotomies are performed proximally enough to allow adequate fixation distally, even
if the apex of the deformity is closer to the distal femur joint surface. If the correction is
performed along the bisector line of the apex of the deformity (Figure 9), the correction will
achieve alignment of the proximal and distal axes; however, an obligatory translation equal to
the distance between the proximal and distal axis lines at the chosen level of the osteotomy

A notable caveat to femoral deformity analysis and planning must be stated. The anatomic axis
or the mechanical axis may be used for planning purposes; however, the two different
techniques should not be mixed. Anatomic axis planning may be more suitable for an isolated

is suitable for most planning purposes.
The challenge with regard to mechanical axis planning for the femur arises in identification of
the proximal mechanical axis for femoral deformity planning, which may be achieved via the
three-line method1 (Figure 10).
Draw the mid-diaphyseal line of the proximal femur. Confirm that the proximal joint angle is
within the normal parameters to avoid a hidden deformity.
Draw a line that starts at the center of the femoral head and is parallel to the mid-diaphyseal
line.
Draw a third line that starts at the center of the femoral head and creates an angle
consistent with the femoral anatomic-mechanical angle noted above (a mean of 7°). This line
is the proximal mechanical axis of the femur.
Figure 10 AP right hip radiographs demonstrate the three-line method for femoral
mechanical axis planning. The red line connecting the midpoint of the purple lines indicates
the mid-diaphyseal line, or the anatomic axis, of the femur. A, The anatomic axis of the

Sagittal Plane
The alignment of the lower extremity in the sagittal plane is evaluated on a full-length lower
extremity lateral radiograph with the knee in maximal extension. If the radiograph is not
obtained with the knee in maximal extension, erroneous assumptions about a knee flexion
contracture may be made. The lower extremity also has a mechanical axis in the sagittal plane,
and it is defined in the same manner as that for the coronal plane—a straight line connecting
the center of the femoral head to the center of the ankle.1,2
The mechanical axis in the sagittal plane should pass just anterior to the hinge point of the
knee. The hinge point of the knee in skeletally mature individuals is the intersection of the
Blumensaat line and the posterior femoral cortex. The hinge point in skeletally immature
patients is the intersection of the physis or the physeal remnant and the posterior femoral
cortex.1
If the mechanical axis passes anterior to the anterior aspect of the distal femur, the lower
extremity is in recurvatum. If the mechanical axis passes posterior to the hinge point, the
lower extremity is in procurvatum. The clinical consequence of a procurvatum deformity is the
constant demand on the quadriceps muscle to maintain an upright position, which may lead
to fatigue, patellofemoral discomfort, and gait disturbance.1
To determine the factors contributing to overall sagittal plane alignment, as described for
coronal plane assessment, each of the bone segments (femur and tibia) must be analyzed
separately.
The joint lines for the sagittal plane are defined as follows1,2 (Figure 11).
For the distal femur, the joint line is defined as a line connecting the anterior and posterior
aspects of the distal femoral physis or physeal scar.
For the proximal tibia, the joint line is defined as a line connecting the anterior and posterior
aspects of the tibial plateau.
For the distal tibia, the joint line is defined as a line connecting the anterior and posterior
beaks of the distal tibia.

In measuring the joint angles for the femur and tibia in the sagittal plane, a few modifications
must be noted. The modified mechanical axis of the femur is defined as a line drawn from
the center of the femoral head to a point on the distal femur joint line at the junction of the
anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of its length1 (Figure 12).
The intersection of the distal femur joint line and the modified mechanical axis of the femur
forms the posterior distal femur joint angle. The modified mechanical axis of the tibia is
defined as a line drawn from a point one-fifth of the length of the total joint line from the
anterior aspect of the line to a point at the center of the distal tibia joint line.
The intersection of the proximal tibia joint line and the modified mechanical axis of the tibia
forms the posterior proximal tibia angle, and the intersection of the distal tibia joint line and
the modified mechanical axis of the tibia forms the anterior distal tibia angle. These modified
points on the distal femur and proximal tibia joint lines represent the location at which the
mid-diaphyseal lines usually intersect the joint line in a normal bone.1

Distal tibia sagittal joint line (red line). (Courtesy of Jeanne M. Franzone, MD, Wilmington, DE.)

Another caveat is important to consider in performing an analysis of the sagittal plane. Given
that the sagittal plane is the plane of motion of the knee, hyperlaxity or soft-tissue contracture
may contribute to or compensate for sagittal plane bony deformity. Analysis of the
contribution of the soft-tissue component of the deformity is predicated on the fact that the
long-leg radiograph is obtained in maximal knee extension.
The anterior cortical line is drawn along the anterior aspect of the femur.

The sagittal plane joint angles are measured as described previously, and the degree of the
deformity is defined as the number of degrees by which each of the joint angles differs from
the normal value.
The soft-tissue contribution to the sagittal plane deformity is calculated as soft-tissue
contribution = anterior cortical line – femoral deformity – tibial deformity1 (Figure 13).

Natural History of Lower Extremity Alignment
The natural history of lower extremity alignment in otherwise healthy children was described
well by Salenius and Vankka5 in a series of 1,480 children. They noted that, in newborns and
children younger than 1 year, the tibiofemoral angle was in varus and then converted to valgus
at age 2 to 3 years. Then it corrected gradually to slight valgus by approximately age 8 years.
Although the tibiofemoral angle is not the most informative assessment of lower extremity
deformity analysis, these data provide a useful framework within which to evaluate and follow
young children.
Consequences of Malalignment
Malalignment of the lower extremity is presumed to contribute to degenerative changes of the
lower extremity joints, given the uneven weight distribution through the joints. McClure and
Herzenberg6 published a literature search on pediatric limb deformity that reviewed the
relationship between malalignment and degenerative changes. McKellop et al7 reported
biomechanical data showing that larger deformities closer to the knee joint increased
pathologic forces across the knee.
In vivo animal studies also have supported varus and valgus malalignment of the lower
extremity as a contributor to degenerative changes of the knee.8,9 McClure and Herzenberg6
described a number of studies presenting cross-sectional clinical data and available clinical
follow-up data on the correction of malalignment.
In a retrospective cohort study of patients with posttraumatic malunion and resulting
malalignment, Visscher et al10 reported that malalignment consistently resulted in more
advanced arthritis scores in the overloaded compartment. The severity of arthritis based on
Osteoarthritis Research Society International grading consistently correlated with the degree
of malalignment and time with deformity after posttraumatic malunion.
Available biomechanical and clinical data indicate that abnormal joint forces because of
deformity are a clinical concern and that realignment may be clinically helpful in symptomatic
individuals.
